figures.cap: quartic graph with single root on negative x-axis and horizontal point of inflection on positive x-axis

solutions.latex:
From the graph: the curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -1$ (a single root) and has a horizontal point of inflection on the $x$-axis at $x = 2$ (a triple root, factor $(x-2)^3$ or $(2-x)^3$).

Both ends of the graph go down, so the quartic has a negative leading coefficient.

$y = (x+1)(2-x)^3$ has roots $-1$ and $2$ (triple), and its leading term is $x\cdot(-x)^3 = -x^4$, which is negative.

Options A and D have roots at $1$ and $-2$; option B has a positive leading coefficient.

figures.cap: graph of a cubic polynomial touching the x-axis at a positive x-value

solutions.latex:
From the graph: the curve crosses the $x$-axis once at a negative value and touches it (a double root) at a positive value. It does not pass through the origin, so the equation is $y = -(x-b)(x-c)^2$, not $y = -x(x-b)(x-c)$.

The single root $b$ is negative and the double root $c$ is positive: $b < 0$, $c > 0$.

(The leading coefficient is negative, matching the curve rising on the left and falling on the right.)

parts.latex: Find the values of $t$ and $h$ at the turning point of the graph.

The graph shows $h=12$ when $t=0$.

What is the other value of $t$ for which $h=12$?

solutions.latex:
The turning point lies on the axis of symmetry, midway between the $t$-intercepts 2 and 6.
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{6+2}{2} \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= 4^2-8\times 4+12 \\ &= -4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds correct value of $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The graph is symmetric about the axis $t=4$. The point $t=0$ is 4 units to the left of the axis, so the other point is 4 units to the right:
$$t=4+4=8$$

768.stem:
The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is dilated vertically by a factor of $q^2$ and then

translated 81 units down, the transformed function is given as

$$g(x)=q^2x^2-81$$

parts.latex: When the transformed function $g(x)$ is translated $p$ units to the left, the resulting function is denoted as $h(x)$. Write an expression for $h(x)$.
Find all possible values of $p$ and $q$ if $h(x)=9x^2+36x-45$.

solutions.latex:
Translating $p$ units to the left replaces $x$ with $x+p$:
$$h(x)=q^2(x+p)^2-81$$

Equate $h(x)$ from (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} q^2(x+p)^2-81&=9x^2+36x-45\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x-45+81\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x+36\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x^2+4x+4)\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
Comparing both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} q^2&=9 & x+p&=x+2\\ q&=\pm3 & p&=2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $p$ or $q$, or equivalent merit
Equates the two expressions for $h(x)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find all points of intersection between $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.

solutions.latex:
The graphs meet where $f(x)=g(x)$. Factorising $x^2-4=(x+2)(x-2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} x-2&=(x+2)(x^2-4)\\ &=(x+2)(x+2)(x-2)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} (x+2)^2(x-2)-(x-2)&=0\\ (x-2)\left[(x+2)^2-1\right]&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x-2=0$ gives $x=2$.

$(x+2)^2=1$ gives $x+2=\pm1$, so $x=-1$ or $x=-3$.

Using $y=x-2$, the points of intersection are $(2,0)$, $(-1,-3)$, $(-3,-5)$.
criteria: Obtains the factorised form, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the vertex of the parabola $y=x^2-6x+10$.

solutions.latex:
The vertex lies on the axis of symmetry, $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=-\dfrac{-6}{2\times 1}\\&=3\end{aligned}$$
$y$-coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=(3)^2-6(3)+10\\&=1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The vertex is $(3,1)$.
criteria: Finds the axis of symmetry, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y=x^2-6$, labelling all intercepts.
On the same set of axes as in part (a), sketch the graph of $y=-2x-3$.
Find algebraically the $x$-coordinates of the two points where the graphs intersect.
Hence solve the inequality $x^2-6<-2x-3$.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{163_q8_s1}

$x$-intercepts, where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=x^2-6\\x^2&=6\\x&=\pm\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}$$
$y$-intercept, where $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=0-6\\&=-6\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{163_q8_s1}

$y$-intercept: $y=-3$.

$x$-intercept, where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-2x-3\\2x&=-3\\x&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

The graphs intersect where the $y$ values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-6&=-2x-3\\x^2+2x-3&=0\\(x+3)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=-3\text{ or }x=1$$

The parabola is below the line between the points of intersection:
$$-3<x<1$$

Characteristics of the cubic function $f(x)$ are given.

\begin{itemize}
\item $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x)$.

parts.latex: A parabola with vertex $(2,-5)$ has a $y$-intercept of 11. Find the equation of the parabola.

solutions.latex:
Vertex form with vertex $(2,-5)$:
$$y=a(x-2)^2-5$$
When $x=0$, $y=11$:
$$\begin{aligned} 11 &= a(0-2)^2-5 \\ 11 &= 4a-5 \\ 16 &= 4a \\ a &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=4(x-2)^2-5$$
(Expanded form $y=4x^2-16x+11$ is also acceptable.)

solutions.latex:
Test $(2,4)$ in $y=2^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4\\\text{RHS}&=2^2\\&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(2,4)$ lies on $y=2^x$.

Test $(2,4)$ in $y=-2x^2+8x-4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4\\\text{RHS}&=-2(2)^2+8\times2-4\\&=4\end{aligned}$$

The vertex lies on the axis of symmetry, $x=\dfrac{-b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{-8}{2\times(-2)}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
From (a), $y=4$ when $x=2$.

$\therefore$ Vertex is $(2,4)$

parts.latex:
For two functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$, it is known that for all $a>0$, $g(a)>h(a)$.

It is also known that $h'(x)<0$ and $g'(x)>0$ for $x>0$.

How many solutions are there to $g(x)-h(x)=0$ in the domain $a>0$?

solutions.latex:
Let $d(x)=g(x)-h(x)$. Then $d'(x)=g'(x)-h'(x)$.

For $x>0$, $g'(x)>0$ and $h'(x)<0$, so $d'(x)>0$.

Also $g(a)>h(a)$ for all $a>0$, so $d(x)>0$ for every $x>0$.

Hence $g(x)-h(x)=0$ has no solution in $x>0$ (the difference never reaches $0$).

meta.self_check: Logical argument: d>0 on the whole domain, so no zero. Agrees with key A (monotonicity is not even needed).

parts.latex: How many solutions are there to the equation $|x+1| = \sin x$ ?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{463_q2_s1}

$|x+1|\ge 0$ and $\sin x\le 1$, so a solution needs $|x+1|=\sin x\le 1$, which means $-2\le x\le 0$, and $\sin x\ge 0$.

On $-2\le x\le 0$, $\sin x\le 0$, with $\sin x=0$ only at $x=0$. But at $x=0$, $|x+1|=1\ne 0$.

So the graphs of $y=|x+1|$ and $y=\sin x$ never meet: there are no solutions.

Find the equation of the polynomial with degree 6.

\exfigure{388_q14_1}

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-1$ (factor to the power $1$), flattens through $x=1$ (power $3$) and touches the axis at $x=4$ (power $2$). The powers add to $6$, matching the degree.

parts.latex:
The parabola $f(x)=-x^2+9mx+2$ has a maximum at $x=\dfrac{2}{m}$, where $m$ is a constant such that $m\neq 0$.

What are the values of $m$?

solutions.latex:
The parabola $f(x)=-x^2+9mx+2$ has its maximum at the axis of symmetry
$$x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=-\dfrac{9m}{2(-1)}=\dfrac{9m}{2}$$
Equate this to $\dfrac{2}{m}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9m}{2} &= \dfrac{2}{m} \\ 9m^2 &= 4 \\ m &= \pm\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The parabola opens downwards for any $m$, so both values give a maximum.
